extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of literature/history; writers and critics interested in representations of heroism
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative principles for creating or analyzing heroic figures and the phenomenon of hero-worship across history and literature; covers what makes a 'great man', how societies receive them, and archetypal heroic roles. Useful for characterisation and thematic treatment of heroism.

rubrics_metrics.name: A man's practical religion as primary fact
rubrics_metrics.description: “A man's religion is the chief fact with regard to him... The thing a man does practically believe (and this is often enough without asserting it even to himself)... that is his religion.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When creating or evaluating a character, foreground their operative beliefs — what they act as if they hold true — rather than mere professed creeds. Show convictions through behaviour and decision-making rather than through rhetorical assertion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Great men as creators/modellers of history
rubrics_metrics.description: “Universal History...is at bottom the History of the Great Men who have worked here. They were the leaders of men, the modellers, patterns, and in a wide sense creators, of whatsoever the general mass of men contrived to do or to attain.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray heroic figures as originating powerful thoughts/actions that reshape their world. Emphasize their creative, formative intellect and leadership rather than treating them as passive reflections of circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heroic radiance: native original insight and nobleness
rubrics_metrics.description: Great men are described as a “living light-fountain” of native original insight, of manhood and heroic nobleness; in whose radiance all souls feel that it is well with them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make a hero's influence palpable: they should inspire, enlighten, and elevate others. Show small characters being improved or steadied by proximity to the hero; suggest an inner luminous quality (not merely public acclaim).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hero-worship as boundless admiration and social glue
rubrics_metrics.description: “Worship of a Hero is transcendent admiration of a Great Man... Loyalty is akin to religious Faith... Society is founded on Hero-worship.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When depicting social dynamics, show how unbounded admiration and allegiance to a hero organize loyalties, ranks, and institutions. Use scenes of reverence and obedience to illustrate social cohesion (or its perversion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat belief-systems as earnest with underlying truth, not mere quackery
rubrics_metrics.description: Carlyle protests the hypothesis that religions arose from quackery; he insists they “have all had a truth in them, or men would not have taken them up.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid dismissive, reductive portrayals of characters' religions or ideologies as mere frauds. Even mistaken beliefs should be given interior logic and felt sincerity; dramatize why followers found them convincing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allegory should be the product, not the origin, of conviction
rubrics_metrics.description: The text argues allegory is generally “a product of the certainty, not the producer of it.” Allegory and poetic symbols follow from prior felt certainties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In narrative, ensure symbolic or allegorical elements arise organically from characters' deep convictions or cultural certainties rather than being imposed superficially. Let symbols emerge from interior truths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evoke primordial wonder and personify natural forces
rubrics_metrics.description: Primitive men experienced Nature as preternatural and personified its forces (e.g., Fire as a demon, Thunder as Thor). Carlyle emphasizes the childlike, open wonder before Nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To convey heroic or mythic atmosphere, use vivid personification of natural phenomena and cultivate a sense of awe. Let environment reflect and amplify a hero's stature or spiritual perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depict man as revelation — the human as temple of the divine
rubrics_metrics.description: “The true Shekinah is Man!... There is but one Temple in the Universe... the Body of Man.” The human being is presented as a revelation of the Highest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characterise heroes as embodiments or revelations of larger spiritual or moral truths. Use physicality and inward depth to suggest that the hero manifests something transcendent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hero as decisive agent (the lightning metaphor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Carlyle likens the great man to lightning that kindles dry fuel; the hero's word is a wise healing word which sets things ablaze into change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show heroes acting decisively and catalytically — moments where a single choice or utterance triggers sweeping transformation. Avoid diffusing agency across faceless historical forces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject portraying heroes as merely ‘creatures of the Time’
rubrics_metrics.description: Carlyle criticises critics who reduce great men to being ‘the creature of the Time’ and insists that great men are often indispensable saviours of their epoch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give heroes meaningful individual initiative and moral/intellectual substance that can alter their era. Resist narrative devices that explain greatness away as mere historical determinism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish authentic heroism from forged social dignities
rubrics_metrics.description: Social dignities are likened to bank-notes representing gold—some are forged; when most are forged, revolutions follow. “We can do with some forged false notes; with a good many even; but not with all, or the most of them forged!”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast genuine, inner greatness with hollow status or manufactured reputations. Dramatic tension can come from exposing forgeries and showing consequences when authentic heroism is lacking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heroic types/archetypes (divinity, prophet, poet, priest, man of letters, king)
rubrics_metrics.description: Carlyle organizes Heroes into six classes — e.g., The Hero as Divinity (Odin), The Hero as Prophet (Mahomet), The Hero as Poet (Dante, Shakespeare), The Hero as Priest (Luther), The Hero as Man of Letters (Johnson), The Hero as King (Cromwell, Napoleon).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing a hero, consider which archetypal role they occupy and adopt the attendant functions and proportions: spiritual revelation, moral lawgiving, imaginative creation, institutional reformation, intellectual authorship, or political leadership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heroes must resonate with cultural values — the crowd’s ideal
rubrics_metrics.description: Using Voltaire as example, Carlyle shows that a people will worship a figure who represents their ideal (he was ‘the realized ideal of every one of them’).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make clear why a culture or group admires a hero by aligning aspects of the character with prevailing values, needs, or self-image; show the mutual fit between hero and society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show endurance of hero-worship across skeptical ages
rubrics_metrics.description: Carlyle insists Hero-worship endures even in times of unbelief and is an 'everlasting adamant' beneath revolutionary wreck.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depict reverence for greatness as a persistent human need that survives ideological change; scenes of private or public veneration can illustrate this continuity even in cynicism.
